intro.text: A number sign (#) is used with this entry because of evidence that auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4) is caused by a heterozygous 430-kb tandem duplication on chromosome 7 that covers most of the HDAC9 gene and includes possible regulatory elements of the neighboring TWIST1 gene.

checks.claim: Auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4) is caused by a heterozygous 430-kb tandem duplication on chromosome 7.
checks.evidence_quote: This study highlights a fourth locus causative of ARCND, represented by a tandem duplication of 430 kb in a candidate region on chromosome 7 defined by linkage analysis.
checks.explanation: The 430-kb tandem duplication on chromosome 7 is reported, but the paper never explicitly states the zygosity (heterozygous).

checks.evidence_quote: The duplication spanned 430 302 bp (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1, covering most of the HDAC9 gene.

checks.evidence_quote: duplicated possible regulatory element sequences within HDAC9, which we demonstrated, through a chromosome conformation capture assay, make contact with the TWIST1 promoter.

paragraphs.text: Auriculocondylar syndrome (ARCND) is a rare disorder affecting structures derived from the first and second pharyngeal arches, mainly resulting in micrognathia and auricular malformations ('question mark ears'). Other features include mandibular condyle hypoplasia, microstomia, glossoptosis, postauricular tags and prominent cheeks, and there is wide clinical variability, including cases with isolated ear anomalies (Romanelli Tavares et al., 2022). ARCND4 is caused by a 430-kb duplication at the HDAC9/TWIST1 locus on chromosome 7, identified in a single large Brazilian family (Romanelli Tavares et al., 2022).

Facial asymmetry, a feature not highlighted in other reports of the disorder, was highly prevalent among the patients.

paragraphs.text: Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) studied a previously reported non-consanguineous 4-generation Brazilian family, which they designated F1, with 11 members showing the typical features of ARCND. Of those documented, most had question mark ears (8 of 10), microstomia (8 of 10), and micrognathia (6 of 10), with considerable intrafamilial variability. The patients did not have large, open fontanelles, the hallmark feature of trisomy 7p.

After excluding 3 loci associated with first and second pharyngeal arch disorders (Treacher Collins syndrome, oculoauriculovertebral spectrum, and Townes-Brocks syndrome), a genomewide search showed evidence of linkage to 1p21.1-q23.3 in F2 (maximum lod score of 3.01 at theta = 0); this locus was not linked to the phenotype in F1, providing evidence for genetic heterogeneity.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of the Brazilian ARCND family F1, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) excluded pathogenic variants in the PLCB4, GNAI3, and EDN1 genes by Sanger sequencing. Whole-exome sequencing of 4 affected individuals identified, within the linkage regions, only a synonymous TRIL variant that did not segregate with the disease. Gene prioritization ranked TWIST1 as the top candidate within the chromosome 7 region, and targeted resequencing of a 2.4-Mb region around TWIST1 revealed no pathogenic variants in TWIST1 but detected a heterozygous tandem duplication of 430,302 bp (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) telomeric to TWIST1 and covering most of the HDAC9 gene. The duplication segregated with the disease in the family (lod score of 2.88). Capture-C analysis using the TWIST1 promoter as viewpoint showed multiple cis interactions between the TWIST1 promoter and possible regulatory elements within the duplicated region.

paragraphs.text: To test pathogenicity, Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) generated induced pluripotent stem cells (iPSCs) from 3 affected family members and controls. Neural crest cells derived from patient iPSCs showed increased HDAC9 (3.15-fold) and TWIST1 (2.03-fold) mRNA expression and a significant decrease in migratory capacity (4.3-fold) compared with controls, whereas cell cycle distribution was not different. Mesenchymal stem cells derived from patient neural crest cells showed significantly diminished alkaline phosphatase activity after 9 days of osteoinduction (20.3-fold decrease) and a subtle decrease in matrix mineralization, indicating delayed or impaired osteogenic differentiation.

paragraphs.text: In affected members of a non-consanguineous 4-generation Brazilian family with auriculocondylar syndrome-4 (ARCND4), Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022) identified a heterozygous 430,302-bp tandem duplication (NC_000007.14:g.18437239_18867540dup) located telomeric to TWIST1 and covering most of the HDAC9 gene. Several HDAC9 transcript isoforms were duplicated in their entirety, whereas full-length catalytically active isoforms extended beyond the breakpoint and were likely disrupted. The duplication was found by targeted resequencing, characterized by breakpoint PCR, and segregated with the disease; all unaffected individuals were negative. Capture-C showed contacts between the TWIST1 promoter and the duplicated region, and patient iPSC-derived neural crest cells showed increased HDAC9 and TWIST1 expression and reduced migration.

agent.process_note: I read the abstract of Masotti et al. (2008), which is the only part available, and the full text of Romanelli Tavares et al. (2022). Neither paper gives a cytogenetic band for the duplication or MIM numbers for HDAC9 or TWIST1, and no HGNC reference data was supplied, so the intro says only 'chromosome 7' and has no gene MIM numbers. Both papers call their family F1 and describe 11 affected members, and Romanelli Tavares call theirs 'previously reported'. Even so, the text I had does not explicitly cite Masotti as the source, so I did not state that the two families are the same. I listed HDAC9 as the gene because it is the one inside the duplication, although the authors suggest that TWIST1 is deregulated. I gave only the features reported for this family, not the general features of ACS.
